notes.body:
The medical analogy in this chapter works in one direction: the physician administers treatment because he is still there, still engaged, still committed to the patient's healing. Burning, cauterization, and amputation are not cruelties — they are the most extreme forms of care, acts of intervention, not abandonment.

The prayer shifts everything. To need burning or amputation "through his turning away" is not to receive a harsher treatment — it is to arrive at irreversible damage because **the treatment itself was never given**. The imam's withdrawal does not inflict spiritual burning; it removes the physician from the room. What remains is the disease, unchecked, the corrupting humors (اَلْكَيْمُوسَات) of the soul — our arbitrary desires, our resistance, our turning away from guidance — spreading and consuming, the way an untreated infection eventually takes the limb that might have been saved.

The Quranic verse the author places immediately before this prayer confirms the logic:

وَلَوْ يُؤَاخِذُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلنَّاسَ بِمَا كَسَبُوا۟ مَا تَرَكَ عَلَىٰ ظَهْرِهَا مِن دَآبَّةٍۢ

If God took humanity to task for what they deserve, He would not leave a single living creature on the surface of the earth.
Fatir 35:45

The mercy of the imams (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) functions as a living buffer between us and the full weight of our own corruption. Their patience with our resistance, their willingness to bear our bad conduct, their looking upon us with an eye of mercy rather than contempt — all of this actively absorbs consequences we have already earned. When that presence is withdrawn, we face what was already ours.

This is what makes the prayer so quietly devastating. To need burning while the physician is present is to be gravely ill but still held within the circle of care. To arrive at that same condition through his turning away is to face it alone.
notes.anchor: those who require burning or the amputation of limbs through his turn…
notes.quote: those who require burning or the amputation of limbs through his turning away from us
etymology: اَلْكَيْمُوسَات (corrupting humors): borrowed into Arabic medical writing from Greek χυμός, meaning juice or fluid. Arabic pluralizes the borrowed root, making كَيْمُوسَات the bodily humors believed to govern health and illness together. The author lifts the term directly into the spiritual register: what corrupts the body's fluids corrupts the soul by the same logic.

التَّسْلِيم (submission): from the root س-ل-م, whose core sense is wholeness and safety — the same root that gives us سَلَام, peace. The word quietly insists that to surrender completely is not to lose something but to become whole; peace, in this root, is never seized but handed over.

notes.body:
Leadership becomes necessary precisely because people cannot reliably know their own good — the animal craves what harms it, the patient resists the medicine that would cure him, the child flees the lessons that would free him. It is a structural condition: the led, by definition, lack the vantage point to see where they are being guided. A guide who shares that same limitation has not solved the problem; he has simply placed one blind person slightly ahead of the others.

The physician analogy makes this sharpest. A person of sound mind accepts a painful prescription because he trusts that the physician sees his condition better than he does. That trust rests entirely on the physician's superior and reliable knowledge — reduce that knowledge, and you reduce the only ground on which obedience to a painful remedy makes sense. Errors in treating the soul are more severe than errors in treating the body. The guide of souls therefore needs not merely more knowledge than the ordinary person has, but a kind that cannot make the catastrophic errors a merely competent guide would make. **Competence is a matter of degree; the need here is for a knowledge that stands outside the limitation it is called to remedy.**

A logical argument runs through the language itself. The title الْإِمَام — the one who stands ahead — cannot belong to the الْمَأْمُوم, the one who follows. Leadership is not a title assigned from outside; it describes a real position in the order of knowing. To appoint a second-best person as imam gives him the name while leaving the actual function of guidance empty.

Appointment by human choice runs into a deeper problem still. If people cannot reliably know their own good — which is the very reason leadership is necessary — **they cannot be trusted to identify who among them best knows it.** The imam's authority cannot rest on the community's election without circularity; it must be grounded in something that stands above the very limitation that made leadership necessary in the first place. That is why the chapter insists the leader must be the most noble, the most perfect, the most knowing — not as an ideal we aspire to, but as the only logical resolution to the problem.
notes.anchor: It is therefore mandatory that this leader be the best of all people:…
notes.quote: It is therefore mandatory that this leader be the best of all people: the most noble, the most perfect, the most knowing, and the most pure
etymology: إمام (imam): from the root أ-م-م, meaning to face toward, to stand in front of, to intend. The word shares its root with أم (mother) — the one toward whom a child orients. The imam is not called a leader by title; the word itself describes being out in front, the one others face toward and move behind.

مأموم (ma'mum): the passive participle of the same root أ-م-م — the one who is faced toward, who is positioned behind. The grammar encodes the relationship structurally: the imam acts and leads; the ma'mum receives and follows. You cannot swap the grammar without destroying the meaning.

تسليم (taslim): from the root س-ل-م, the same root as سلام (peace) and سلامة (wholeness, safety). Submission here is not passive defeat; it is the act of entering into wholeness — aligning with what is truly good so that nothing in us works against our own wellbeing.

عقل (aql): from the root ع-ق-ل, meaning to tether or hobble an animal so it does not stray. Reason is the faculty that binds the self to what is real and keeps it from wandering into harm — which is why the Universal Intellect الْعَقْلُ الْكُلِّي is, by this logic, the one who keeps all creation from straying.
